Vertical & Horizontal Formatting

Organize files into a readable narrative and keep lines concise so each statement is easy to scan.

Duration: 12-minute live coding
In this lesson

How to group related lines, use blank lines for logical paragraphs, and break long lines and signatures for readability.

Why it matters

Better formatting reduces search time, lowers mistakes in edits, and helps teams read intent without heavy context switching.

Quick example

Group related declarations, keep helper functions near their callers, and break parameter lists across lines.

Visual concept
Vertical flow
Group related lines, separate blocks with blank lines, order high-level before details.

Limit line length, break signatures at commas or operators, keep consistent operator spacing.

def process_customer_order(customer_id, product_id, quantity, shipping_address_line1, shipping_address_line2, shipping_city, shipping_zip, payment_method, discount_code):
    # Retrieve customer details

    # Calculate total price

    if discount_code == "SAVE10": total_price *= 0.9
    # Prepare shipping information
    shipping_info = f"{shipping_address_line1}, {shipping_address_line2}, {shipping_city}, {shipping_zip}"
    # Process payment

    # Log order

screens.title: Vertical Formatting — The Narrative Flow
screens.narratorSegment: Vertical formatting arranges code along the vertical axis so a reader can follow a narrative from top to bottom. Think of your file as an article: high-level definitions first, then supporting details and helper functions. The key claims are vertical density — keep related lines close — and blank-line separation — insert visual paragraphs between distinct ideas. For example, group variable declarations used by a block directly above that block instead of scattering them across the file. A concrete pattern is to place setup or initializations, then a blank line, then the main loop or processing, then another blank line for cleanup or logging. A common misconception is that fewer blank lines mean more compact code; in reality, removing all separators forces the reader to spend mental cycles discovering boundaries. Another anti-pattern is placing a helper function far away from its only caller: that increases vertical distance and causes needless search. Your takeaway: use vertical grouping to reduce context switching, and insert blank lines to mark conceptual breaks. When you refactor, ask whether the next line continues the same idea or starts a new paragraph of logic.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Vertical Formatting
Definition

Vertical Density & Blank Lines

Keep related lines adjacent and use blank lines to mark logical paragraphs or separate different responsibilities.

Rule: Group related declarations
Place variables and small helpers close to the code that uses them so readers don't have to search.
Example: Before vs After
# Bad vertical density:
def process_data(data):
    user_id = data.get("user_id")

    user_name = data.get("name")

    # Some complex processing logic
    processed_result = user_id + user_name # Simplified for example

    # More unrelated logic
    log_entry = f"Processed {user_id}"
    print(log_entry)

    return processed_result

# Good vertical density:
def process_data_clean(data):
    user_id = data.get("user_id")
    user_name = data.get("name") # Related declarations grouped

    processed_result = user_id + user_name # Core logic

    log_entry = f"Processed {user_id}" # Logging logic
    print(log_entry)

    return processed_result
Why it helps
  • Reduces time spent searching for related code.
  • Makes the procedural narrative explicit: setup, process, cleanup.
  • Helps reviewers locate logical boundaries quickly.
Key Takeaway

Use blank lines to create paragraphs and keep functions readable top-to-bottom.

Common mistake

Removing all blank lines to be brief; this increases cognitive load as readers must infer boundaries.

screens.title: Using Blank Lines to Create Logical Paragraphs
screens.narratorSegment: A simple process helps decide where to insert blank lines. First, identify setup code: imports, configuration, and initializations. Second, identify core processing: loops, transformations, or the main algorithm. Third, identify side effects and cleanup: logging, input and output, or return packaging. Use a blank line to separate these conceptual blocks. For example, in a function that retrieves data, validates it, computes results, and logs, place a blank line after initialization before the loop, another blank line before logging, and a final line before returning. A practical misconception is to place blank lines only for visual comfort; instead, place them at concept boundaries so they carry meaning. When a helper function serves only one caller, keep it adjacent to reduce vertical distance. As you refactor, ask whether the next few lines continue the same idea; if not, insert a separation. This process turns a dense function into readable paragraphs and makes reasoning about each phase simpler. Try applying this to a messy function and note how scanning time drops. Using Blank Lines to Create Logical Paragraphs means separate setup, core processing, and cleanup with blank lines so each block communicates a single concept.. In practical terms, a practical pattern for separating setup, processing, and cleanup. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Blank-Line Process
Process

Three-step separation

  1. Setup: imports, config, variable initializations used by the rest of the function.
  2. Core processing: loops, transforms, and the main algorithmic steps.
  3. Side-effects & return: logging, I/O, packaging results, and the return statement.
Why this reduces cognitive load

Readers can focus on one conceptual block at a time, which speeds comprehension and reduces mistakes during edits.

Annotated example
def do_work(items):
    config = load_config()
    result = []

    for i in items:
        processed = transform(i)
        result.append(processed)

    log_summary(result)
    return result
Check your understanding

Given a function, mark where setup ends and processing begins. If unclear, consider extracting a helper.

screens.title: Vertical Distance & Ordering
screens.narratorSegment: Vertical distance refers to how far apart conceptually related pieces of code appear in the file. When a helper function is only used by a single higher-level function, it should be defined adjacent to that caller or immediately after it. This reduces vertical distance and the need to jump around. Ordering is the complementary idea: higher-level constructs first, helpers and details later. For example, public methods or class interfaces typically precede private helpers so the reader sees the A P I intent before implementation. A common mistake is scattering related declarations across a file to satisfy an artificial personal ordering preference; this increases the reader's search cost. Another misconception is that ordering always equals top-down execution; ordering is about logical prominence and discoverability. Practically, keep two rules in mind: keep related items near each other and present the reader with the high-level story before low-level details. This reduces context switching during code review and documentation reading. Vertical Distance & Ordering means reduce vertical distance and order by prominence so readers encounter the high-level narrative before low-level details.. In practical terms, place related helpers close and high-level concepts before details. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Distance & Ordering
Principle

Place helpers near callers; show intent first

Keep the code a short walk: when items are conceptually connected, put them physically close in the file.

Pattern: API then implementation
Show public methods or class surface first, helpers and details afterward so readers see the big picture immediately.
Anti-pattern
Scattering one function's supporting variables and helpers across distant parts of the file; this forces search and increases error risk.
Concrete tip

If a helper has only one caller, consider defining it immediately below or above that caller; if it has broad use, centralize it in a utilities area.

Key Takeaway

Reduce vertical distance for related code and present high-level concepts before the implementation details.

screens.title: Horizontal Formatting — Line Length & Breaking
screens.narratorSegment: Horizontal formatting focuses on the readability of each line. The primary rule is to respect a line length limit — often 80 to 120 characters — and break long lines at logical boundaries: after commas in parameter lists, after operators in expressions, or before a long string concatenation. For example, a function with many parameters should be broken so each parameter or small group of parameters is on its own line with consistent continuation indentation. A common pitfall is breaking lines arbitrarily in the middle of a semantic unit, which hides intent. Another misconception is that longer lines save vertical space; they often force horizontal scrolling and make diffs harder to read. When breaking, align continuation lines to clearly indicate their relationship to the original line. The goal is that a single glance reads the meaning of the line without scanning horizontally. Think of each line as a sentence: if it becomes too long, break it into readable clauses. Horizontal Formatting — Line Length & Breaking means limit line length and break at natural logical points so each line remains a clear, scannable unit of meaning.. In practical terms, keep each line scannable by limiting width and breaking at logical points. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Line Length & Breaking
Definition

Limit and Break

Break long signatures and expressions at commas or operators and indent continuation lines to show association.

Good pattern
def send_notification(user_email, subject, message_body,
                      attachment_path, priority_level, sender_name):
    # ...
Why it matters
  • Keeps diffs compact and readable.
  • Avoids horizontal scrolling when reading code.
  • Makes parameters and operators visible at a glance.
Common mistake

Breaking at arbitrary characters that split semantic units, which obscures meaning rather than clarifying it.

screens.title: Breaking Long Function Signatures
screens.narratorSegment: Function signatures with many parameters are a common horizontal formatting problem. The recommended approach is to break the parameter list across lines, ideally after commas or by grouping related parameters, and to indent continuation lines consistently so they are clearly part of the same signature. For example, instead of a single long line, place the opening parenthesis on the first line, then list parameters on subsequent lines indented one level, and close the parenthesis on its own line aligned with the def. This shows each parameter as a visible item and reduces horizontal scanning. A misconception is to cram parameters into multiple short lines with inconsistent indentation; inconsistent indentation makes it hard to tell where the signature ends and the body begins. In practice, prefer this pattern even if it increases vertical height; readability and clear diffs are worth the extra lines. content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Breaking Signatures
Example

Refactor a long signature

Before (too long):
def send_notification(user_email, subject, message_body, attachment_path, priority_level, sender_name):
    # ...
After (broken at commas):
def send_notification(
    user_email,
    subject,
    message_body,
    attachment_path,
    priority_level,
    sender_name,
):
    # ...
Guidelines
  • Break after commas or logical groups.
  • Indent continuation lines consistently.
  • Place closing parenthesis on its own line when helpful for clarity.
Check

Can a reader see each parameter without horizontal scrolling? If not, break the list.

screens.title: Horizontal Alignment — Trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: Horizontal alignment aligns similar elements vertically — for example assignment operators or parameter names — so a block of declarations lines up visually. This can make patterns pop and speed visual scanning. However, alignment is brittle: adding a longer identifier or changing a value often requires adjusting whitespace across many lines, which creates noisy diffs and extra reformatting. The chapter shows two approaches: manual alignment and a formatter-friendly, left-aligned style. Manual alignment can be useful for small, stable blocks where entries rarely change. Formatter-friendly left alignment is more robust for evolving code. A common misconception is that alignment always improves clarity; in many collaborative projects, it causes merge churn. The practical rule: use alignment sparingly and only when it genuinely improves readability without creating constant maintenance overhead. Prefer a consistent formatter and reserve manual alignment for stable, intentional tables of related items. content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Alignment Trade-offs
Manual alignment (can be brittle)
user_id          = "abc"
user_name        = "Alice"
user_email       = "alice@example.com"
user_permissions = ["read", "write"]
Nice to scan, but adding a long field forces realignment across lines and noisy diffs.
Formatter-friendly (robust)
user_id = "abc"
user_name = "Alice"
user_email = "alice@example.com"
user_permissions = ["read", "write"]
Easier diffs and consistent with automatic formatting tools, at the cost of a slightly less tabular visual.
Guideline

If the block is small and stable, manual alignment can help. For evolving code, prefer formatter-friendly styles to minimize maintenance churn.

screens.title: Operator Spacing & Punctuation

Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Starter Refactor

Refactored example

An annotated refactor showing blank lines and a broken signature.

def process_customer_order(
    customer_id,
    product_id,
    quantity,
    shipping_address_line1,
    shipping_address_line2,
    shipping_city,
    shipping_zip,
    payment_method,
    discount_code,
):
    # Retrieve customer details
    customer_data = {"id": customer_id, "name": "John Doe"}  # Simplified

    # Validate product availability
    product_available = True  # Simplified
    if not product_available:
        raise ValueError("Product not available")

    # Calculate total price
    unit_price = 10.50  # Simplified
    total_price = unit_price * quantity
    if discount_code == "SAVE10":
        total_price *= 0.9

    # Prepare shipping information
    shipping_info = (
        f"{shipping_address_line1}, {shipping_address_line2},"
        f" {shipping_city}, {shipping_zip}"
    )

    # Process payment
    payment_successful = True  # Simplified
    if not payment_successful:
        raise ValueError("Payment failed")

    # Log order
    print(
        f"Order processed for {customer_data['name']} for {quantity} of {product_id} "
        f"at {total_price} to {shipping_info} via {payment_method}."
    )

    return {"order_id": "ORD123", "status": "completed", "total": total_price}
Why this helps

Each block is now a clear paragraph; the signature is visible and shipping construction is readable without long lines.

Common mistake

Putting raises inline or keeping everything on one line to save space; this hides control flow and increases reading cost.

screens.title: Common Anti-patterns and Misconceptions
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson catalogs common anti-patterns to avoid. First, excessive vertical cramming: removing blank lines everywhere to make a function shorter visually, which forces readers to infer boundaries. Second, scattered helpers: placing supporting functions or variables far from their sole caller, increasing vertical distance. Third, brittle alignment: manually aligning many lines that will change frequently, creating noisy diffs. Fourth, arbitrary line breaking: splitting semantic units in the middle of a logical expression so intent is obscured. Fifth, inconsistent operator spacing that makes expressions harder to parse at a glance. For each anti-pattern, the corrective action is simple: restore meaningful blank lines, move helpers near callers or extract shared utilities, prefer formatter-friendly styles over fragile alignment, break lines at logical points, and standardize spacing via a formatter. A practical misconception is that these rules are stylistic preferences without measurable impact; in practice, they reduce cognitive load and improve review speed. Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Anti-patterns

Common Anti-patterns

Vertical cramming

Removing blank lines to shorten a file hides conceptual boundaries and increases cognitive load.

Scattered helpers

Placing a helper far from its only caller creates unnecessary vertical distance and search time.

Brittle alignment

Manual alignment may look nice but creates noisy diffs when fields change length.

Arbitrary line breaks

Breaking a semantic unit mid-expression obscures meaning; break only at logical boundaries.

Corrective actions
  • Restore meaningful blank lines and group related lines.
  • Move helpers close to callers or centralize truly shared utilities.
  • Prefer formatters; use manual alignment only for stable tables.
  • Break lines at commas and operators, and standardize operator spacing.

Module 7 › Chapter 6.7 › Quick Reference
1. Blank-line paragraphs

Separate setup, core logic, and cleanup with blank lines so each block is a single idea.

2. Break long lines

Break signatures and expressions at commas or operators and indent continuations for clarity.

3. Align with care

Use manual alignment only when stable; otherwise prefer formatter-friendly layouts.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we treat the appearance of code as a communication tool. You will learn how vertical formatting — grouping related lines, ordering definitions, and inserting blank lines — creates a readable narrative through a file. You will also learn horizontal techniques like limiting line length, breaking long signatures and expressions, and judicious alignment and spacing so each line reads like a clear sentence. These changes reduce cognitive load, let reviewers scan intent faster, and prevent awkward edits that introduce bugs. For example, grouping variable declarations with the logic that uses them reduces the need to search for definitions. Breaking a very long parameter list into multiple lines makes each parameter visible without horizontal scrolling. We will practice with a Python function that initially mixes unrelated steps and long signatures, then refactor it using vertical and horizontal principles. By the end you will be able to spot vertical-density problems, apply blank-line separation, break long lines sensibly, and weigh alignment trade-offs. Ready to make code more humane to read?

By the end of this chapter you will apply vertical formatting to group related code elements and use blank lines to separate distinct concepts within a file. You will understand horizontal formatting limits so you can prevent excessively long lines and make code easier to scan. You will practice aligning related lines selectively — for example parameters or assignment lists — to enhance clarity without creating brittle whitespace. Finally, you will learn to identify anti-patterns in both axes of formatting that reduce readability and increase maintenance cost. Each objective combines a practical skill and a reason why it matters in team code: fewer mistakes during edits, faster code review, and clearer intent for future maintainers. We'll practice these skills on Python examples, refactoring an overly compact function into clear paragraphs and sensible line breaks. Expect to explain your choices and recognize when alignment helps versus when it becomes brittle.

In addition to understanding the principles, you'll practice refactoring a Python function that mixes unrelated steps and has a very long parameter list. The hands-on activity asks you to add blank lines to create logical paragraphs, break the function signature across lines with clear indentation, and correct inconsistent operator spacing. You'll also evaluate small alignment choices for readability and stability. Finally, an assessment question asks you to identify at least two vertical-format improvements and explain why they help, and to show how to break a long parameter list in a readable way. These exercises let you apply the rules on real code, which is where the benefits appear: faster reviews, fewer merge conflicts due to whitespace churn, and clearer intent for new team members. We'll also highlight common anti-patterns so you know what to avoid when refactoring.

Vertical formatting arranges code along the vertical axis so a reader can follow a narrative from top to bottom. Think of your file as an article: high-level definitions first, then supporting details and helper functions. The key claims are vertical density — keep related lines close — and blank-line separation — insert visual paragraphs between distinct ideas. For example, group variable declarations used by a block directly above that block instead of scattering them across the file. A concrete pattern is to place setup or initializations, then a blank line, then the main loop or processing, then another blank line for cleanup or logging. A common misconception is that fewer blank lines mean more compact code; in reality, removing all separators forces the reader to spend mental cycles discovering boundaries. Another anti-pattern is placing a helper function far away from its only caller: that increases vertical distance and causes needless search. Your takeaway: use vertical grouping to reduce context switching, and insert blank lines to mark conceptual breaks. When you refactor, ask whether the next line continues the same idea or starts a new paragraph of logic.

A simple process helps decide where to insert blank lines. First, identify setup code: imports, configuration, and initializations. Second, identify core processing: loops, transformations, or the main algorithm. Third, identify side effects and cleanup: logging, input and output, or return packaging. Use a blank line to separate these conceptual blocks. For example, in a function that retrieves data, validates it, computes results, and logs, place a blank line after initialization before the loop, another blank line before logging, and a final line before returning. A practical misconception is to place blank lines only for visual comfort; instead, place them at concept boundaries so they carry meaning. When a helper function serves only one caller, keep it adjacent to reduce vertical distance. As you refactor, ask whether the next few lines continue the same idea; if not, insert a separation. This process turns a dense function into readable paragraphs and makes reasoning about each phase simpler. Try applying this to a messy function and note how scanning time drops. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Vertical distance refers to how far apart conceptually related pieces of code appear in the file. When a helper function is only used by a single higher-level function, it should be defined adjacent to that caller or immediately after it. This reduces vertical distance and the need to jump around. Ordering is the complementary idea: higher-level constructs first, helpers and details later. For example, public methods or class interfaces typically precede private helpers so the reader sees the A P I intent before implementation. A common mistake is scattering related declarations across a file to satisfy an artificial personal ordering preference; this increases the reader's search cost. Another misconception is that ordering always equals top-down execution; ordering is about logical prominence and discoverability. Practically, keep two rules in mind: keep related items near each other and present the reader with the high-level story before low-level details. This reduces context switching during code review and documentation reading. Vertical Distance & Ordering means reduce vertical distance and order by prominence so readers encounter the high-level narrative before low-level details.. In practical terms, place related helpers close and high-level concepts before details. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Horizontal formatting focuses on the readability of each line. The primary rule is to respect a line length limit — often 80 to 120 characters — and break long lines at logical boundaries: after commas in parameter lists, after operators in expressions, or before a long string concatenation. For example, a function with many parameters should be broken so each parameter or small group of parameters is on its own line with consistent continuation indentation. A common pitfall is breaking lines arbitrarily in the middle of a semantic unit, which hides intent. Another misconception is that longer lines save vertical space; they often force horizontal scrolling and make diffs harder to read. When breaking, align continuation lines to clearly indicate their relationship to the original line. The goal is that a single glance reads the meaning of the line without scanning horizontally. Think of each line as a sentence: if it becomes too long, break it into readable clauses. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Function signatures with many parameters are a common horizontal formatting problem. The recommended approach is to break the parameter list across lines, ideally after commas or by grouping related parameters, and to indent continuation lines consistently so they are clearly part of the same signature. For example, instead of a single long line, place the opening parenthesis on the first line, then list parameters on subsequent lines indented one level, and close the parenthesis on its own line aligned with the def. This shows each parameter as a visible item and reduces horizontal scanning. A misconception is to cram parameters into multiple short lines with inconsistent indentation; inconsistent indentation makes it hard to tell where the signature ends and the body begins. In practice, prefer this pattern even if it increases vertical height; readability and clear diffs are worth the extra lines. Horizontal alignment aligns similar elements vertically — for example assignment operators or parameter names — so a block of declarations lines up visually. This can make patterns pop and speed visual scanning. However, alignment is brittle: adding a longer identifier or changing a value often requires adjusting whitespace across many lines, which creates noisy diffs and extra reformatting. The chapter shows two approaches: manual alignment and a formatter-friendly, left-aligned style. Manual alignment can be useful for small, stable blocks where entries rarely change. Formatter-friendly left alignment is more robust for evolving code. A common misconception is that alignment always improves clarity; in many collaborative projects, it causes merge churn. The practical rule: use alignment sparingly and only when it genuinely improves readability without creating constant maintenance overhead. Prefer a consistent formatter and reserve manual alignment for stable, intentional tables of related items. Operator spacing and punctuation are subtle but powerful horizontal details. Consistent spacing around operators like equals, plus, and comparison operators greatly improves the eye's ability to parse expressions. The chapter contrasts well-spaced code versus cramped code. For example, write 'if x == 5:' and 'y = a + b', not 'if x==5:' or 'y=a+b'. Consistent spacing also helps when scanning code for operators during reviews. Punctuation such as commas and colons should be followed by a single space to mark separation. A common misconception is that whitespace is insignificant; while Python ignores many extra spaces, humans do not. Poor spacing increases the likelihood of misreading an expression, especially in complex conditionals. This lesson catalogs common anti-patterns to avoid. First, excessive vertical cramming: removing blank lines everywhere to make a function shorter visually, which forces readers to infer boundaries. Second, scattered helpers: placing supporting functions or variables far from their sole caller, increasing vertical distance. Third, brittle alignment: manually aligning many lines that will change frequently, creating noisy diffs. Fourth, arbitrary line breaking: splitting semantic units in the middle of a logical expression so intent is obscured. Fifth, inconsistent operator spacing that makes expressions harder to parse at a glance. For each anti-pattern, the corrective action is simple: restore meaningful blank lines, move helpers near callers or extract shared utilities, prefer formatter-friendly styles over fragile alignment, break lines at logical points, and standardize spacing via a formatter. A practical misconception is that these rules are stylistic preferences without measurable impact; in practice, they reduce cognitive load and improve review speed. Let's summarize the key concepts to remember. Vertical formatting is about arranging code top-to-bottom: group related lines, create blank-line paragraphs, and place high-level items before details. Vertical density means keeping logically connected lines physically close so readers don't have to search. Horizontal formatting is about each line: respect line length limits, break long signatures and expressions at commas or operators, and keep consistent operator spacing. Horizontal alignment can help scanning but can be brittle, so apply it sparingly or rely on formatters. These ideas work together: vertical structure provides the narrative, and horizontal clarity makes each sentence readable. Keep this checklist in mind during refactors and aim for readable diffs.
